query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating ceramic and graphite reinforcement particles into a CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will promote the formation of a dual-phase microstructure that dynamically generates a stable, self‐lubricating tribofilm, thereby lowering both friction and wear rate across the temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: An unreinforced CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy exhibiting increasing friction and wear—especially at elevated temperatures—due to limited intrinsic self‐lubrication and wear resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled volume fraction (e.g., around 10–20 wt%) of ceramic particles (such as WC) combined with graphite particles into the CoCrFeNi matrix to create a composite.
generation.conditions: Sliding tests performed using ball-on-disk experiments under varying loads and sliding speeds in ambient or controlled environments, covering the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A composite microstructure in which hard ceramic particles provide dispersion strengthening and wear resistance, while graphite particles contribute to the formation of a lubricious carbon-based tribofilm during sliding.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the ceramic reinforcement enhances hardness and load-bearing capacity, mitigating abrasive wear. With increasing temperature, the graphite becomes active, generating a continuous lubricious tribofilm that reduces shear strength at the sliding interface, thus lowering the friction coefficient and wear rate. The synergy between the two types of particles is expected to maintain stable tribological performance across the full temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The reinforced composite is predicted to exhibit a reduction in both the coefficient of friction (by roughly 20–30%) and the wear rate (potentially an order-of-magnitude improvement) compared to the unreinforced CoCrFeNi alloy, across varying loads and temperatures up to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the unreinforced CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, which tends to show higher friction and accelerated wear, particularly under elevated temperature conditions due to inadequate self-lubricating behavior.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to hold under moderate to high sliding loads in ambient or mildly oxidative environments and within the operational temperature range up to 800 °C. Extreme oxidative environments or conditions exceeding 800 °C may introduce additional challenges that are not addressed by this intervention.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal volume fraction of reinforcements and their distribution require further optimization. Additionally, the temperature-dependent activation of graphite lubrication and potential issues with particle agglomeration introduce uncertainty in the absolute magnitude of the tribological improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples—with and without the 10–20 wt% ceramic/graphite reinforcement mixture—keeping all processing and surface finishing conditions identical. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding tests at various loads and across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
measurements: Coefficient of friction during sliding at each temperature condition
Wear rate quantified via mass loss or volumetric measurements
Characterization of the worn surface and tribofilm formation using microscopy and spectroscopy methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if, under identical test conditions, the reinforced samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate compared to the unreinforced CoCrFeNi alloy, or if no corresponding lubricious tribofilm is observed on the worn surfaces.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.

Intrigued by the extensive lubricious behavior of the HEA in ethanol, a further study has been conducted to analyze the capabilities of HEA nanoflakes in other solvents like water. The (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 powder is combined with distilled water at a concentration of 1.5g L−1. This water‐based lubricant solution was sonicated for thorough mixing (≈9 h sonication time) and spray coated uniformly onto the steel disk for ball‐on‐disk friction experiments across all loads from 1 N to 9 N. The results found all sliding tests to fail within short distances (Figure S5, Supporting Information). In Figure S5 (Supporting Information), the starting COF decreases with an increase in load, showing the intrinsic HEA behavior like in the case of HEA in ethanol. However, the HEA in water exhibits limited wear resistance and high wear rates in the magnitude of 10−6 mm3 (N∙m)−1 as compared to HEA in ethanol which has wear rates in the magnitude of 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1. This shows that the ethanol solvent plays a significant role in increasing the tribological performance of HEA during friction tests.
